DNA Viruses MICROBIOLOGY LE 2 · interactive reviewer

Lecture map p. 1

  • Non-enveloped DNA viruses: Parvoviridae, Adenoviridae, Papillomaviridae, Polyomaviridae.
  • Enveloped DNA viruses: Herpesviridae, Poxviridae, Hepatitis B virus.
  • The lesson repeatedly connects viral structure → replication → tissue tropism → clinical disease → diagnosis → treatment and prevention.

Fast orientation p. 1

  • Parvovirus B19: erythroid progenitor tropism and fifth disease.
  • Adenovirus: respiratory, ocular, gastrointestinal and urinary epithelial disease.
  • HPV: epithelial infection with benign warts or malignancy depending on type.
  • Herpesviruses: lifelong persistence with latency and possible reactivation.
  • Poxviruses: large DNA viruses that complete replication in the cytoplasm.
  • HBV: partially double-stranded DNA with reverse transcription during replication.

Red-exclamation points in the lecture are treated as high-yield.
This reviewer repeats those points in the final Cram Sheet and keeps their qualifiers intact.

Parvoviridae: structure, tropism and replication p. 1

Core properties p. 1

  • Parvoviruses are the smallest DNA viruses. The lecture links the name to the Latin word parvus, meaning small.
  • They are naked, icosahedral viruses with single-stranded linear DNA.
  • Parvovirus B19 is the pathogenic human parvovirus emphasized in the lecture.
  • B19 has marked tropism for erythroid progenitor cells and is approximately 20 nm in diameter.
  • Virions are highly resistant to inactivation. They remain stable from pH 3 to 9 and can withstand 56°C for 60 minutes.
  • Lecture-listed inactivating agents include formalin, beta-propiolactone and oxidizing agents such as oxygen, hydrogen peroxide and chlorine.

Why host S phase matters p. 1

Parvoviruses depend heavily on host-cell functions for DNA replication in the nucleus.

  • The virus enters by endocytosis, then reaches the nucleus.
  • It cannot induce the host cell to enter S phase.
  • It must remain in the nucleus until the host cell enters S phase on its own.
  • Once that happens, the infected cell is directed to synthesize viral DNA.
  • Capsid proteins accumulate in the nucleus, empty capsids form, genomes are packaged, and completed virions are released by cell lysis.
Key differentiator
B19 is difficult to culture.
Only primary erythroid progenitors are permissive for infection.
The cellular receptor emphasized in the lecture is the blood-group P-antigen or globoside.

Cellular receptor and rapidly dividing tissues p. 2

  • P-antigen is expressed on mature erythrocytes, erythroid progenitors, megakaryocytes, endothelial cells, placenta, fetal liver and fetal heart.
  • The lecture highlights B19 propensity to infect rapidly dividing tissues.

Pathogenesis, transmission and epidemiology p. 2

Pathogenesis chain p. 2

  • Main targets are immature erythroid lineage cells.
  • Major replication sites include the bone marrow, some blood cells and the fetal liver.
  • Viral replication causes cell death and interrupts red-cell production.
  • This produces erythrocyte maturation arrest with erythroblast intranuclear inclusions.
  • Persistent infection in immunocompromised patients can produce chronic anemia.
  • Severe fetal anemia can culminate in fetal death.

Routes and epidemiology p. 2

  • The usual portal of entry is the respiratory tract.
  • Transmission may also occur through blood transfusion, infected blood products such as coagulation factors, and vertical transmission from mother to fetus.
  • Infections occur year-round, in all age groups, and can appear as school outbreaks.
  • Childhood infection is common. Spread among siblings and among children in schools or daycare centers is emphasized as a major transmission setting.
  • During pregnancy, the mother’s older child is a common source of maternal infection.

Clinical illnesses p. 2

Must know
Erythema infectiosum or fifth disease is the most common manifestation of parvovirus B19.

Erythema infectiosum: timing and rash p. 2

  • Common in children, with a lecture-stated peak of 5 to 18 years.
  • Transmission is usually by respiratory droplets. Vertical and blood-borne transmission are also possible.
  • Incubation is usually 1 to 2 weeks.
  • A short viremia begins around 7 to 10 days after exposure and lasts about one week. During viremia, virus can be detected in nasal washes and gargle specimens.
  • Prodrome may include mild fever, malaise, coryzal symptoms, nausea, headache, diarrhea and myalgia.
  • The illness has a biphasic rash. Intense malar erythema produces the classic slapped-cheek appearance.
  • Once antibody production has occurred at this stage, the immunocompetent patient is described as no longer infectious.
  • A fine lacy maculopapular rash then appears on the trunk and limbs and usually fades in 2 to 4 days.
  • Adults may develop arthralgia, especially women. The lecture describes a symmetrical small-joint arthritis of the hands or fingers that may persist for weeks to months.
B19 disease patterns that are easy to confuse
SettingLecture disease or outcomeMechanistic anchor
ImmunodeficiencyPersistent B19 with chronic marrow suppression. Pure red cell aplasia.Failure to clear B19 permits prolonged suppression of erythropoiesis.
PregnancyNon-immune fetal hydrops or fetal loss from severe anemia.Maternal-fetal transmission is most common with high maternal plasma viral loads.
Sickle cell anemia or thalassemiaTransient, abrupt disruption of erythropoiesis produces an aplastic crisis.Baseline high red-cell turnover makes abrupt erythroid arrest clinically important.

Diagnosis, treatment and prevention p. 2

Diagnosis p. 2

  • PCR can detect viral DNA in serum, blood cells, tissues and respiratory secretions.
  • IgM can become positive from 7 to 10 days after exposure and indicates recent infection.
  • IgG appears from about 15 days after exposure.
  • In immunodeficient patients with chronic infection, antibodies may be absent. The lecture therefore emphasizes viral DNA detection in this setting.

Treatment and prevention p. 3

  • Severe anemia may require blood transfusion.
  • Commercial immunoglobulin preparations contain neutralizing antibodies and may be used for persistent B19 infection in immunocompromised patients.
  • Prevention measures listed include handwashing, facemask use and avoiding shared drinking glasses or straws.
Must know
There is no vaccine and no antiviral drug available against human parvovirus in this lecture.

Adenoviridae: structure, types and transmission p. 3

Core properties and named serotypes p. 3

  • Adenoviruses are naked, icosahedral viruses with double-stranded linear DNA.
  • They occur worldwide and are present year-round.
  • Spread may occur through fecal-oral transmission, respiratory droplets, contaminated fomites and hand-to-eye transfer.
  • Respiratory: types 1, 2, 3, 5 and 7.
  • Gastroenteritis: types 40 and 41.
  • Military recruits and young adults in group settings: types 3, 4 and 7 are common.
  • Swimming-pool conjunctivitis: types 3 and 7. The lecture describes this as waterborne and more common in summer.
Adenovirus structural elements
StructureLecture function
FiberProjects from the 12 penton bases.
Contains type-specific antigens used in serotyping.
Associated with hemagglutinating activity.
Penton baseHas toxin-like activity that can rapidly produce cytopathic effects and detach cells from the surface.
Exhibits a group-reactive antigen.

Replication and immune-evasion effects p. 3

Early phase p. 3

  • Replication is best in epithelial cells.
  • The fiber mediates attachment and the virus is internalized into endosomes.
  • Uncoating begins in the cytoplasm and is completed in the nucleus.
  • The host cell is induced to enter S phase, creating conditions for viral replication.
  • Early viral functions protect the infected cell from host defenses and produce gene products needed for DNA replication.
  • Viral DNA replication occurs in the nucleus.

Late phase p. 3

  • The late phase begins with onset of viral DNA synthesis.
  • Late genes encode structural proteins synthesized in the cytoplasm.
  • Capsomeres assemble into empty capsids in the nucleus. Naked DNA enters the preformed capsid.
  • The lecture states that about 100,000 virus particles may be produced per cell.
  • Virions are released by host-cell lysis.

Adenovirus effects on host defense p. 3

  • Viral-associated RNA or vaRNA is a non-coding RNA that protects the virus from antiviral effects of interferons.
  • The E3 region protein can inhibit cytolysis of infected cells.
  • E3 gp19 kDa blocks movement of MHC class I antigens to the host-cell surface, protecting infected cells from cytotoxic T-lymphocyte-mediated lysis.
Exam anchor
vaRNA is the adenovirus non-coding RNA that protects against interferon antiviral effects.

Pathogenesis and clinical illnesses p. 4

Pathogenesis p. 4

  • Adenoviruses infect and replicate in epithelial cells of the respiratory tract, eyes, gastrointestinal tract and urinary tract.
  • They usually do not spread beyond regional lymph nodes.
  • Adenoviruses 1 to 7 are the most common serotypes worldwide and account for most adenovirus-associated illness.
Must know
One adenovirus serotype can cause different clinical diseases.
More than one serotype can cause the same clinical illness.
Respiratory and ocular adenovirus syndromes
SyndromeSerotypes or settingKey lecture details
Acute febrile pharyngitisGroup C viruses, especially 1, 2 and 5.Common in infants and children.
Cough, sore throat, nasal congestion and fever.
May resemble other respiratory viral infections.
Acute respiratory diseaseTypes 4 and 7, occasionally type 3.Epidemics among new military recruits.
Crowding, fatigue and exposure to new strains are emphasized.
Vaccination has been used for military personnel.
Pharyngoconjunctival feverTypes 3 and 7.School-age children.
Also called swimming-pool conjunctivitis.
Mild ocular involvement with pharyngeal respiratory illness.
Conjunctivitis lasts about 1 to 2 weeks without lasting sequelae.
Epidemic keratoconjunctivitisTypes 8, 19 and 37.More serious and highly contagious, mainly in adults.
Redness, tearing, foreign-body sensation and keratitis.
Corneal subepithelial opacities may persist for up to 2 years.

Respiratory disease in infants and children p. 4

  • The lecture attributes about 5% of acute respiratory disease in young children to adenoviruses.
  • Disease occurs year-round and is described as most prevalent from winter to summer.
  • Types 3, 7 and 21 are linked to 10% to 20% of pneumonia in childhood.
  • Incubation period is 3 to 10 days.
  • Transmission occurs by small droplets or larger aerosols.
  • Testing is by culture or nucleic acid amplification, depending on laboratory capability.

Gastrointestinal, urinary and transplant-associated disease p. 4

  • Types 40 and 41 are associated with infantile gastroenteritis and may account for 5% to 15% of viral gastroenteritis in young children. They are abundant in diarrheal stools.
  • Types 1 to 7 may cause respiratory disease in transplant patients that can progress to severe pneumonia or fatal disseminated infection.
  • Pediatric liver transplant recipients may develop adenovirus hepatitis in the allograft.
  • Pediatric heart transplant recipients may develop myocardial adenovirus infection and have increased risk of graft loss.
  • Hematopoietic stem-cell transplant recipients can be infected by many adenovirus types.
  • AIDS patients may develop gastrointestinal and other infections.
  • Some serotypes cause acute self-limited hemorrhagic cystitis, especially in males, with hematuria and recoverable virus in the urine.

Resistance, diagnosis and prevention p. 5

Resistance to clinical disease p. 5

  • Protection correlates with circulating neutralizing antibodies, which may persist for life.
  • Type-specific antibodies can protect against disease symptoms but do not always prevent reinfection.
  • Adenovirus infections are often asymptomatic.
  • Maternal antibodies usually protect infants against severe adenovirus respiratory disease.
Adenovirus diagnostic methods
MethodWhat the lecture uses it for
PCRDetection in respiratory samples, blood, tissue and body fluids.
Immunofluorescence with antihexon antibodyIdentification of virus in infected cells. Hexon is described as the largest and most abundant capsid protein.
Hemagglutination inhibition and neutralizationMeasurement of type-specific antigens and identification of serotypes.
Direct basal epithelial-cell stainingDetection of viral antigens.
Electron microscopy, ELISA, latex agglutinationDirect examination of fecal extracts for enteropathogenic adenovirus.
Complement fixationCan detect any member of the group.
A fourfold or greater antibody-titer rise from acute to convalescent phase can indicate recent infection.

Treatment and prevention p. 5

  • The lecture states no specific treatment.
  • Handwashing is the simplest preventive measure.
  • Surfaces may be disinfected with sodium hypochlorite.
  • Single-use paper towels are advised during outbreaks because repeatedly used towels may serve as a source.
  • Swimming-pool chlorination can reduce waterborne adenoviral conjunctivitis outbreaks.

Papillomaviridae: properties and disease spectrum p. 5

Core virology and transmission p. 5

  • Papillomaviruses are naked viruses with icosahedral nucleocapsids and supercoiled double-stranded circular DNA.
  • The lecture states that the family is divided into 16 genera.
  • Transmission requires direct contact with infected persons, including sexual contact, or contact with contaminated surfaces and fomites such as communal bathroom floors.
  • All papillomaviruses produce hyperplastic epithelial lesions in their host species.
  • HPVs have strong tissue and cell specificity and infect only the surface epithelia of skin and mucous membranes.
HPV types and lecture associations
HPV type or groupAssociation
16 and 18Lesions can progress to malignancy.
Responsible for more than 70% of cervical cancers, with HPV 16 most common.
HPV 16 is linked to oropharyngeal cancers.
6 and 11Cause about 90% of anogenital warts.
Cause laryngeal papillomas in children.
1, 2, 3 and 4Common cutaneous wart types emphasized in the lecture.
13 and 32Oral and nasopharyngeal mucosal infection, usually benign papillomas.
Must know
HPV genital infections are the most common viral infections of the reproductive tract in the lecture.
HPV is linked to more than 99% of cervical cancers and more than 80% of anal cancers.
All HPV-associated cancers occur more frequently in persons with HIV/AIDS.

Replication follows epithelial differentiation p. 5

  • HPV is highly tropic for epithelial cells of skin and mucous membranes.
  • Viral nucleic acids can be found in basal stem cells.
  • The replication cycle parallels keratinocyte differentiation.
  • Early genes are expressed first, then the viral genome multiplies, then progeny virions assemble in the most superficial layers of the wart.

HPV pathogenesis and malignant progression p. 6

From epithelial infection to malignancy p. 6

  • HPV infection occurs at cutaneous and mucosal sites.
  • Clinical results include common, plantar and flat warts, anogenital warts, laryngeal papillomas and cancers of the cervix, vulva, penis, anus, and some head and neck sites.
  • Genital HPV is sexually transmitted.
  • Progression to malignancy is emphasized especially for warts on mucosal surfaces.
  • Persistent infection with a high-risk HPV is a necessary component of malignant progression in the lecture.
  • Infection is non-lytic and restricted to epithelium, helping shield HPV from the host immune response.
Must know mechanism
High-risk HPV early proteins bind p53 and retinoblastoma protein or pRb.
The lecture links stronger binding affinity to higher malignant-progression risk.
E6 and E7 are the primary oncoproteins in high-risk HPV. They manipulate cell-cycle regulators, induce chromosomal abnormalities and block apoptosis.

Clinical illnesses p. 6

Cutaneous warts and epidermodysplasia verruciformis p. 6

  • Common cutaneous warts are mainly associated with HPV 1, 2, 3 and 4.
  • Common warts are seen on fingers, hands and plantar surfaces. Flat warts may occur on the arms, face and knee.
  • Epidermodysplasia verruciformis is described as a genetic condition that predisposes to numerous warts that fail to regress and spread to many body sites.
  • These lesions may develop into squamous cell carcinoma years later, especially in sun-exposed areas.

Oral and genital tract infection p. 6

  • Oral and nasopharyngeal mucosal infection is associated with HPV 13 and 32 and usually produces benign papillomas.
  • About 30 HPV types can infect the genital tract.
  • HPV 6 and 11 cause 90% of genital papillomas and produce condyloma acuminata. These are described as large, usually benign and often spontaneously regressing.
  • HPV 16 and 18 are associated with a large proportion of cervical cancers.
  • High-risk HPV types are also linked to anal, penile, vaginal, vulvar and oropharyngeal cancers.

Diagnosis, treatment and prevention p. 6

Diagnosis p. 6

  • Cutaneous warts are usually diagnosed by visual inspection.
  • Biopsy may be used when the diagnosis is uncertain, the patient is immunocompromised, or the lesion is pigmented and ulcerated.
  • The lecture states that there is no tissue-culture system for HPV.
  • Typing uses quantitative DNA amplification or PCR.
  • For HPV-associated cancers and precancerous lesions, the lecture emphasizes Pap smear for cervical screening regardless of vaccination status.

Treatment and prevention p. 7

  • Lecture-listed lesion removal includes surgery, cauterization, liquid nitrogen, laser vaporization and cytotoxic chemicals such as podophyllin and trichloroacetic acid.
  • These approaches may remove the wart but HPV may remain in surrounding tissue, allowing recurrence.
  • Patient-applied anogenital wart treatments listed are imiquimod, podofilox and sinecatechins 15% ointment.
  • Provider-administered options listed are cryotherapy, surgical removal, trichloroacetic acid and dichloroacetic acid.
  • Oral interferon has been shown in the lecture to cause regression of laryngeal papillomas.
  • Because infection is transmitted by direct inoculation, avoiding contact with wart tissue is the primary preventive measure. Standard sexually transmitted disease prevention measures apply to genital warts.
Must know vaccine
Gardasil is the lecture-listed vaccine against common HPV types.
It contains capsids from HPV 6 and 11 and HPV 16 and 18.
The lecture notes that it was originally recommended for young females and is now recommended for young males as well.

Polyomaviridae: BKV, JCV and Merkel cell polyomavirus p. 7

Human polyomaviruses in this lecture p. 7

  • Human polyoma virus 1 or BK virus.
  • Human polyoma virus 2 or JC virus.
  • Merkel cell polyomavirus or MCPyV.
  • The lecture notes that the lecturer used the initialism MCV for Merkel-cell polyomavirus. The transcript uses MCPyV to avoid confusion with molluscum contagiosum virus.
  • Droplets from the upper respiratory tract can transmit JCV and BKV. Contact with infected urine may also transmit them.
  • Infection usually occurs in childhood.

This lecture section focuses on transmission and clinical illnesses for BKV, JCV and MCPyV.
It does not provide a dedicated diagnostic-method or treatment regimen for these three viruses, so none is added here.

Herpesviridae: family framework p. 7

Family properties p. 7

  • Herpesviruses are enveloped, icosahedral viruses with double-stranded linear DNA.
  • The envelope is derived from the host nuclear membrane and contains viral glycoprotein spikes.
  • Between envelope and capsid lies the tegument, an amorphous proteinaceous layer containing virus-encoded enzymes and transcription factors needed to initiate infection.
  • A defining property is the ability to establish lifelong persistent infection.
  • Periodic reactivation can occur and is more frequent in elderly and immunosuppressed patients.

Three biologic subfamilies p. 7

  • Alphaherpesvirinae: rapid cytocidal or lytic growth. Latency in nerve ganglia. HSV-1, HSV-2 and VZV.
  • Betaherpesvirinae: slow replication. Multinucleated giant host cells. Latency mainly in non-neural, lymphoreticular and glandular tissues. HCMV, HHV-6 and HHV-7.
  • Gammaherpesvirinae: replicate in mucosal epithelium, then establish latency in B cells and can induce proliferation or immortalization. EBV and HHV-8. The lecture also notes HHV-8 latency and immortalization in endothelial cells.

Replication sequence p. 8

  • Adsorption: envelope glycoproteins bind cellular receptors.
  • Entry: the viral envelope fuses with the host-cell membrane.
  • The capsid is transported through the cytoplasm to a nuclear pore.
  • After uncoating, viral DNA associates with the nucleus and forms a circle.
  • New viral DNA is packaged into preformed empty nucleocapsids in the nucleus.
  • The virus acquires an envelope by budding through the nuclear membrane.
  • Completed virions are carried in a vacuole to the cell surface.
Must know
The productive lytic herpesvirus cycle ends in cell death.
The lecture attributes this to shut-off of most cellular synthetic pathways during viral replication.

HSV-1 and HSV-2: transmission, latency and reactivation p. 8

Transmission and tissue entry p. 8

  • HSV transmission occurs through direct contact with virus-containing secretions, cutaneous lesions and mucosal lesions.
  • Oropharyngeal infection is primarily HSV-1. Virus is shed in saliva. The major modes named are kissing and fingers contaminated with saliva.
  • Genital tract infection is primarily HSV-2. Virus is present in genital secretions. Major routes are sexual intercourse and passage of newborns through the infected birth canal.
  • Both types multiply in epithelial cells at mucosal surfaces and produce vesicles or shallow ulcers that contain infectious virus.
Must know latency map
Oropharyngeal HSV → trigeminal ganglia.
Genital HSV → sacral ganglia.

Reactivation p. 8

  • Infectious virions enter sensory neurons and establish lifelong latent infection in regional ganglia.
  • Provocative stimuli listed are axonal injury, fever, physical or emotional stress and ultraviolet light.
  • After reactivation, virus moves along axons back to peripheral skin or mucosa, where replication resumes.
Must know risk group
Immunocompromised patients are at increased risk of severe HSV infection.
The lecture includes malnutrition, renal, cardiac and bone-marrow transplant recipients, hematologic malignancies and AIDS.

HSV clinical illnesses p. 8

Primary versus recurrent infection p. 8

  • Primary infection occurs in persons without antibodies. It may be subclinical but still induces antibody formation and latency in sensory ganglia.
  • Recurrent lesions are common.

Oropharyngeal disease p. 8

  • Primary HSV-1 disease includes oropharyngeal disease, gingivostomatitis and fever sores.
  • Most primary HSV-1 infections are asymptomatic.
  • Symptomatic gingivostomatitis is most frequent in children around 1 to 5 years.
  • Incubation is about 3 to 5 days. Clinical illness lasts around 2 to 3 weeks.
  • Fever, sore throat, vesicular or ulcerative lesions, malaise and gingivostomatitis may occur.
  • Swollen, tender gums are described as the most striking and common lesion.
  • In adults, primary infection commonly causes pharyngitis and tonsillitis.
  • Recurrent disease produces fever sores, usually clusters of vesicles at the lip border. Pain fades over 4 to 5 days, followed by pustular and crusting stages and healing without scarring.

Keratoconjunctivitis p. 9

  • HSV can cause severe keratoconjunctivitis.
  • Recurrent ocular disease may appear as dendritic keratitis, corneal ulcers or eyelid vesicles.
  • Repeated keratitis can opacify the corneal stroma and may lead to blindness.

Genital herpes p. 9

  • More often caused by HSV-2, although HSV-1 can also cause genital disease.
  • Painful vesiculoulcerative lesions may involve the penis, cervix, vulva, vagina and perineum.
  • Associated findings include fever, malaise, dysuria and inguinal lymphadenopathy.
  • Complications include extragenital lesions and aseptic meningitis.
  • Viral shedding persists for about 3 weeks.
  • HSV-1 and HSV-2 are antigenically cross-reactive. Initial HSV-2 disease is often less severe in a patient already immune to HSV-1.
  • Recurrences are common but usually milder.
  • Virus shedding means the patient can transmit infection to sexual partners.
  • Genital HSV increases acquisition of HIV infection because of ulcerative mucosal lesions.

Herpetic skin infection p. 9

  • Skin infection is uncommon in otherwise healthy persons.
  • Herpetic whitlow: lesions on fingers of dentists and hospital personnel after contamination of abrasions.
  • Herpes gladiatorum: body lesions in wrestlers.
  • Extensive infection can become severe and life-threatening in patients with skin disorders such as eczema or burns.
  • Eczema herpeticum is described as a primary infection, usually HSV-1, in a person with chronic eczema. It can be fatal.

Meningitis and encephalitis p. 9

  • Herpesvirus infection can produce severe meningitis or encephalitis.
  • The lecture describes HSV-1 as the most common cause of sporadic fatal encephalitis in the United States.
  • Mortality is high, and survivors may have residual neurologic deficits.

Neonatal herpes p. 9

  • Neonatal HSV can be acquired in utero, during birth or after birth. The mother is the most common source.
  • The most common route is contact with herpetic lesions while passing through the birth canal. The lecture mentions cesarean delivery in pregnant women with genital herpes lesions to avoid this exposure.
  • Postnatal sources may include infected family members and hospital personnel who are shedding virus.
  • Most neonatal herpes in the lecture is attributed to HSV-2.
  • Three disease categories are described: localized skin-eye-mouth disease, encephalitis with or without skin involvement, and disseminated multiorgan disease including the CNS.
  • The worst prognosis is with disseminated disease. The lecture cites 80% mortality.
  • Primary maternal infection before 20 weeks of gestation is associated with spontaneous abortion.

HSV diagnosis, treatment and prevention p. 10

HSV diagnostic methods
MethodLecture use
PCR or NAATDetect virus in vesicle swabs, blood and CSF.
Sensitive and specific.
CSF PCR is the test of choice and gold standard for herpes meningitis and encephalitis because of sensitivity and rapid turnaround.
Virus cultureCommonly used for mucocutaneous disease.
Virus may be isolated from lesions, respiratory samples, tissues and body fluids during primary infection and asymptomatic periods.
Giemsa-stained vesicle scrapingRapid cytologic method showing multinucleated giant cells.
This finding can indicate HSV-1, HSV-2 or VZV.
SerologyNeutralization, immunofluorescence and ELISA are listed.

Treatment and prevention p. 10

  • Maternal antibodies are passively transferred but are lost during the first 6 months. Greatest susceptibility to primary herpes infection is described from 6 months to 2 years.
  • Antibodies after primary infection do not prevent latent infection or reactivation, but may modify subsequent disease.
  • Acyclovir, valacyclovir and vidarabine are lecture-listed antivirals.
  • Mechanism: inhibition of viral DNA synthesis.
  • These drugs suppress manifestations, shorten healing time and reduce genital-herpes recurrences.
  • Patients with genital herpes should be counseled that asymptomatic shedding occurs. Transmission risk can be reduced by antiviral therapy and condom use.

Varicella-zoster virus or HHV-3 p. 10

One virus, two disease states p. 10

  • HHV-3 causes both chickenpox or varicella and herpes zoster.
  • Varicella is the acute disease after primary contact with VZV.
  • Herpes zoster is reactivation of latent VZV in a partially immune host.
  • Varicella is a highly contagious childhood disease with generalized vesicular eruption of skin and mucous membranes. Disease is more severe in adults and immunocompromised patients.
  • Spread occurs through airborne droplets and direct contact.
  • Zoster is sporadic, especially in older or immunocompromised patients, and produces a painful vesicular rash in the distribution of a sensory ganglion.
Must know
Varicella = primary VZV disease.
Zoster = reactivation of latent VZV in sensory ganglia.

Varicella pathogenesis and clinical pattern p. 10

Varicella sequence p. 10

  • Virus enters through upper-respiratory mucosa or conjunctiva.
  • Primary viremia follows infection and replication in nearby lymph nodes.
  • Secondary viremia follows replication in the liver and spleen.
  • Infected mononuclear cells carry virus to the skin, producing the characteristic rash.
  • The lecture names VZV protein ORF 61 as an antagonist of the beta-interferon pathway.
  • Incubation is 10 to 21 days.
  • Malaise and fever are followed by rash that begins on the trunk, then involves face, limbs, and buccal and pharyngeal mucosa in a centrifugal pattern.
  • Fresh vesicles appear in crops, so macules, papules, vesicles and crusts can be present at the same time.

Varicella complications and immunity p. 10

  • Complications are uncommon in normal children and mortality is very low.
  • Rare encephalitis can be life-threatening and may leave permanent sequelae in survivors.
  • Varicella pneumonia is rare in healthy children but is the most common complication in neonates, adults and immunocompromised patients in the lecture.
  • Neonatal varicella acquired from the mother just before or after birth may disseminate widely and can be fatal.
  • Pediatric leukemia patients are prone to severe disseminated VZV disease.
  • Previous varicella infection is believed to confer lifelong immunity to varicella.

Herpes zoster p. 11

Dermatomal reactivation p. 11

  • Zoster involves acute inflammation of sensory nerves and ganglia, often only one ganglion.
  • Skin lesions follow the innervation of the affected dorsal-root ganglion, producing a dermatomal distribution.
  • The lecture proposes that waning immunity permits ganglionic replication, producing inflammation and pain. Virus then travels down the nerve to the skin and forms vesicles.
  • Cell-mediated immunity is the most important host defense against VZV.
  • Zoster is often unilateral. The trunk, head and neck are commonly involved.
  • The ophthalmic division of cranial nerve V is involved in 10% to 15% of cases.
Key complication
Postherpetic neuralgia is the most common zoster complication in the elderly.
Pain may persist for months and is especially common after ophthalmic zoster.

Severe disease p. 11

  • Visceral disease, especially pneumonia, can cause death in immunosuppressed patients with zoster.

VZV diagnosis, treatment and prevention p. 11

Diagnosis p. 11

  • VZV can be detected from tissue, blood, CSF and body fluids.
  • Tzanck smear examines material from the base of a vesicle for multinucleated giant cells.
  • Direct fluorescent antibody detects viral proteins in clinical material.
  • NAAT is the most sensitive method and the gold-standard assay in the lecture. It is recommended for CSF and other sources.
  • Virus can still be detected in crusting lesions when a vesicle is absent.
  • Blood may be useful in immunocompromised patients with suspected disseminated zoster without the characteristic rash.
  • Culture may be used but requires DNA confirmation.
VZV treatment regimens in the lecture
DrugDose and frequency
Acyclovir800 mg five times daily for 7 to 10 days.
Famciclovir500 mg three times daily for 7 days.
Valacyclovir1 g by mouth three times daily for 5 to 7 days.
Must know timing
Antiviral therapy should be started as soon as possible, within 24 to 48 hours of symptoms.

Prevention and special treatment points p. 11

  • Neonates and immunocompromised patients with severe infection should be treated.
  • Varicella-zoster immune globulin is used to prevent illness after exposure in high-risk patients. The lecture states that it has no therapeutic value once varicella has started.
  • Acyclovir can prevent systemic disease in immunosuppressed patients and halt zoster progression in adults.
  • Lecture-listed alternatives include valacyclovir, famciclovir and foscarnet.
  • A live attenuated varicella vaccine is available and is described as 95% effective at preventing severe disease.
  • A herpes-zoster vaccine is also listed. The lecture describes it as a more potent version of varicella vaccine and recommends it for older adults and people with chronic medical conditions.

Epstein-Barr virus or HHV-4 p. 11

Transmission, targets and latency p. 11

  • EBV spreads through bodily fluids, especially saliva. Saliva contains virus during primary infection and during repeated asymptomatic shedding.
  • EBV causes infectious mononucleosis, also called mono or the kissing disease.
  • The initial replication site is oropharyngeal epithelium.
  • Progeny virus then infects B lymphocytes.
  • The B-cell receptor highlighted in the lecture is the complement component C3d receptor.
  • During B-cell infection, only a limited number of early proteins are synthesized. Their expression leads to latency and B-cell immortalization.
  • EBV early genes induce cell multiplication rather than cell death, leading to polyclonal B-cell proliferation and nonspecific increases in total IgM, IgG and IgA.
EBV-associated malignancies and proliferative disease
AssociationLecture description
Burkitt lymphomaB-cell lymphoma that may present as a jaw tumor in African children and young adults.
Most African tumors contain EBV DNA.
Nasopharyngeal carcinomaEpithelial-cell cancer described as common in males of Chinese and Southeast Asian descent.
EBV DNA is regularly found in tumor cells.
Hodgkin lymphomaEBV genome can be detected in malignant Reed-Sternberg cells.
Non-Hodgkin lymphomaThe lecture states that all CNS non-Hodgkin lymphomas are associated with EBV.
Gastric carcinomaListed among EBV-associated malignancies.
Immunodeficiency-related lymphoproliferative diseaseTransplant and immunodeficient patients may develop monoclonal B-cell lymphomas.
AIDS patients are susceptible to EBV-associated lymphomas and oral hairy leukoplakia.

Pathogenesis and infectious mononucleosis p. 12

Pathogenesis p. 12

  • Primary infection usually begins with infected saliva reaching the oropharynx.
  • Virus replicates in epithelial cells or surface B lymphocytes of the pharynx and salivary glands.
  • Infected people may shed low levels of virus for weeks to months.
  • Infected B cells spread infection throughout the body.
  • Most infected cells are eliminated in immunocompetent hosts. A small number of latently infected lymphocytes persist for life.
  • Primary infection in children is usually subclinical. In young adults it often produces acute infectious mononucleosis.
  • Latent infection can reactivate. Reactivation is usually clinically silent but increases virus in saliva and EBV DNA in blood cells.
  • Immunosuppression may permit clinically important reactivation.
Must know triad
Infectious mononucleosis classical triad:
Fever
Pharyngitis
Lymphadenopathy, usually anterior and posterior cervical nodes.

Infectious mononucleosis p. 12

  • Incubation is 4 to 7 weeks.
  • Splenomegaly and elevated liver enzymes may occur, followed by headache and malaise lasting several weeks.
  • Complete recovery may take much longer.
  • Circulating white-cell count rises with lymphocyte predominance.
  • Many circulating cells are large atypical T lymphocytes called Downey cells.

EBV diagnosis and treatment p. 13

EBV diagnostic markers
Test or markerLecture interpretation or use
Heterophile antibodyRed blood cells or latex agglutination detect anti-erythrocyte antibodies generated during polyclonal B-cell expansion in mononucleosis.
Anti-VCAIgG and IgM antibodies.
Anti-EAIgG antibody.
Anti-EBNAIgG antibody.
EBER in-situ hybridizationGold standard for tissue detection in this lecture.
More sensitive than IHC because EBER is produced regardless of stage of infection or latency.
Quantitative NAATProvides viral load.
Higher loads correlate with greater probability of post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder.

Treatment and prevention section in the lecture p. 13

  • The lecture lists acyclovir 800 mg orally five times daily for 10 days plus prednisolone 0.7 mg/kg daily for 4 days.
  • Acyclovir reduces oropharyngeal shedding while the drug is being given, but does not reduce the number of EBV-immortalized B cells.
  • The lecture states that it has no effect on infectious-mononucleosis symptoms and no proven benefit for EBV-associated lymphomas in immunocompromised patients.
  • Treatment showed no significant benefit for duration of general illness, sore throat, weight loss or absence from school or work.

Cytomegalovirus or HHV-5 p. 13

Core properties and cytopathic effect p. 13

  • CMV belongs to the Betaherpesvirinae.
  • It has worldwide distribution and high seroprevalence, reaching nearly 100% in the elderly population in the lecture.
  • Most childhood and adult infections are asymptomatic. Disease becomes especially important in immunocompromised hosts.
  • CMV has the largest genetic content among the human herpesviruses in the lecture.
  • CMV can bind the Fc portion of immunoglobulins, which helps infected cells evade immune elimination.
  • Human CMV is species-specific and cell-type-specific. Animals cannot be infected with human CMV.
  • Characteristic cytopathic changes include perinuclear cytoplasmic inclusions, intranuclear inclusions, enlarged cytomegalic cells and multinucleation.
  • The classic intranuclear inclusion is the owl’s-eye inclusion.

Transmission and pathogenesis p. 14

Transmission routes p. 14

  • Transmission requires close contact with virus-bearing material.
  • Incubation is 4 to 8 weeks.
  • Children may be asymptomatic but can shed virus for months in many body fluids. The lecture emphasizes saliva as the most common source.
  • Adults may transmit CMV sexually through semen and vaginal secretions, through organ transplantation and blood transfusion, and through breast milk to neonates.
  • Neonates may acquire CMV in utero, during vaginal delivery or through breast milk.
  • Both primary and reactivated maternal infection can cross the placenta. The lecture states that about one third of pregnant women with primary infection transmit virus.

Systemic pathogenesis p. 14

  • Initial replication in respiratory and gastrointestinal epithelium is followed by viremia and infection of organs throughout the body.
  • In symptomatic cases, commonly affected organs include kidney tubule epithelium, liver and CNS.
  • CMV has been isolated from lung, liver, esophagus, colon, kidney, monocytes, and T and B lymphocytes.
  • It can produce an infectious-mononucleosis-like syndrome.
  • CMV establishes lifelong latency and can be shed intermittently from the pharynx and urine long after primary infection.
  • Primary infection can depress cell-mediated immunity.
  • Reactivated infection is much more important in immunocompromised patients than normal hosts.
  • High-risk groups include hematopoietic stem-cell and solid-organ transplant recipients, patients receiving chemotherapy and AIDS patients.
  • The lecture emphasizes pneumonia and colitis as common complications.
  • A distinctive feature is repeated episodes of asymptomatic virus shedding over prolonged periods.

Clinical disease and congenital CMV p. 14

Key differentiator
CMV mononucleosis-like illness lacks heterophile antibodies.
This is the major distinguishing feature from EBV infectious mononucleosis in the lecture.

Mononucleosis-like illness p. 14

  • Adult primary infection may cause persistent fever, muscle pain and lymphadenopathy.
  • Laboratory abnormalities listed include anemia, thrombocytopenia, elevated abnormal lymphocytes, abnormal liver-function tests and elevated liver enzymes.
  • The lecture also lists positive rheumatoid factor and antinuclear antibody levels.
  • Organ involvement is uncommon in immunocompetent hosts.

Opportunistic CMV disease p. 14

  • CMV is an important opportunistic pathogen in HIV infection and in solid-organ or bone-marrow transplant recipients.
  • Disease entities listed include hepatitis, retinitis, esophagitis, colitis, pneumonitis, polyradiculopathy, transverse myelitis and subacute encephalitis.
  • CMV retinitis is described as having a pizza-pie appearance on ophthalmic examination.
Must know congenital CMV
HCMV is the most common intrauterine viral infection in the lecture.
Congenital disease is called cytomegalic inclusion disease.
Severity is greatest when infection occurs during the first trimester.

Congenital disease p. 15

  • Damage may involve liver, spleen, blood-forming organs and the nervous system, and can progress to fetal death.
  • Jaundice, petechiae and hepatosplenomegaly are the most frequently noted clinical findings in symptomatic infants in the lecture.
  • Nervous-system injury is linked to hearing loss and mental retardation.
  • CMV is included in the lecture’s TORCH group with toxoplasma, others such as syphilis and hepatitis B, rubella, CMV and herpes simplex.
  • Lecture mnemonic for congenital CMV: Chorioretinitis, Microcephalia and mental/motor retardation, periVentricular calcifications.

CMV in immunocompromised hosts p. 15

Transplant and HIV disease p. 15

  • Transplant recipients may acquire HCMV from transplanted tissue, leukocytes in transfused blood or reactivation of endogenous latent virus.
  • GI tissue destruction, hepatitis and pneumonia are common.
  • Pneumonia is a major cause of death in bone-marrow transplant recipients in the lecture.
  • HCMV infection is associated with decreased survival of solid-organ transplants such as heart, liver and kidney.
  • HCMV coinfection is frequent in HIV due to shared transmission routes and may accelerate AIDS pathology.
  • CMV pneumonia and blindness from retinitis are especially common, although all organ systems may be affected.
  • Other significant problems listed are encephalitis, dementia, esophagitis, enterocolitis and gastritis.

CMV diagnosis, treatment and prevention p. 15

CMV diagnosis
MethodLecture interpretation
NAATStandard test in the lecture.
PCRDetects virus in blood, CSF, saliva and urine.
Quantitative viral load helps predict CMV disease in immunocompromised patients.
Higher loads favor systemic disease.
A negative blood PCR has high negative predictive value for systemic disease.
HistopathologyLarge cells with owl’s-eye nuclear inclusions.
SerologyUsed for past or present infection in immunocompetent patients and for serostatus before transplant.
Recent infection may show a fourfold IgG rise or IgM.
Monoclonal antibodiesCan detect virus-positive leukocytes.
Human fibroblast cultureUsed for isolation. Virus can be recovered from tissue, body fluids, throat washings and urine.
CMV treatment and prevention points
Agent or measureLecture use
GanciclovirLife-threatening CMV in immunosuppressed patients.
Decreases severity of retinitis, esophagitis and colitis.
Early treatment reduces disseminated disease in bone-marrow allograft recipients.
Controls progressive hearing loss in neonates with congenital infection.
Cidofovir and foscarnetCMV retinitis and ganciclovir-resistant strains.
Acyclovir and valganciclovirLecture notes some benefit in bone-marrow and renal-transplant patients.
PreventionIsolate newborns with generalized cytomegalic inclusion disease from other newborns.
Test transplant donors and recipients for CMV antibody.

HHV-6: roseola infantum p. 15

Clinical anchor p. 15

  • HHV-6 causes sixth disease, roseola infantum or exanthem subitum.
  • Most infections occur in the first 3 years of life.
  • A sudden high fever of about 39°C to 40°C lasts around 3 to 5 days.
  • The defining sequence is that an erythematous macular rash appears when the fever goes away.
  • The rash often begins on the chest, back and abdomen, then spreads to the neck and arms and may reach the legs and face.
Must know
Roseola: high fever first, then erythematous macular rash as the fever disappears.
HHV-6 variants
VariantLecture description
HHV-6AImplicated in progression of HIV disease to AIDS.
Transactivates HIV transcription and accelerates cell death in coinfected cells.
HHV-6BUbiquitous.
Major cause of roseola infantum.
Associated with febrile seizures in children.

Pathogenesis, diagnosis and treatment p. 16

  • HHV-6 genome organization resembles HCMV.
  • It infects peripheral-blood lymphocytes and cells of several solid organs.
  • HHV-6 infects lymphoid cells through the cellular receptor human CD46.
  • Reactivation is common in transplant patients and during pregnancy. The lecture states that it occurs in about half of patients undergoing hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation.
  • Transmission is probably through oral secretions from infected carriers.
  • NAAT is more sensitive than serology for acute infection.
  • The lecture states that HHV-6 is not detected in plasma or serum unless infection is active or the virus is chromosomally integrated.
  • Lecture-listed treatment: ganciclovir, cidofovir and foscarnet.

HHV-7 p. 16

Roseola-related but often asymptomatic p. 16

  • HHV-7 can cause sixth disease or roseola infantum, but infection is more often asymptomatic.
  • Primary infection has been linked to roseola in infants and children.
  • Most infections occur in childhood, later than the very early age typical for HHV-6.
  • Persistent infection is established in the salivary glands, and virus can be isolated from saliva in most individuals.

HHV-8 or Kaposi sarcoma herpesvirus p. 16

Kaposi sarcoma and other disease p. 16

  • HHV-8 is also called Kaposi sarcoma herpesvirus or KSHV.
  • Kaposi sarcoma is a vascular tumor with mixed cellular composition.
  • The lecture describes soft purplish plaques and papules that form nodules, typically beginning on the feet and ankles and spreading across legs, hands and arms.
  • Tumors can also develop internally and cause severe internal bleeding.
  • The lecture additionally presents an alternative hypothesis that Kaposi sarcoma represents multicentric hyperplasia with lymphatic-venular anastomoses and elements of both lymphatic and blood-vessel endothelium.
  • HHV-8 is also involved in the pathogenesis of body-cavity-based lymphomas in AIDS patients.

Transmission, diagnosis and treatment p. 16

  • Transmission routes listed are oral secretions as the most common route, sexual transmission, transplacental mother-to-child transmission, blood, organ transplantation and breast milk.
  • Laboratory diagnosis: PCR or serology using indirect immunofluorescence, Western blot or ELISA.
  • Lecture-listed treatment: foscarnet, famciclovir, ganciclovir and cidofovir.

Poxviridae: structure, replication and immune evasion p. 16

Core properties p. 16

  • Poxviruses are oval or brick-shaped with surface ridges.
  • They contain a core and lateral bodies.
  • The genome is a single linear molecule of double-stranded DNA.
  • Virions contain enzymes used in early replication steps and are highly resistant to inactivation.
  • Viral proteins help evade host immune-defense systems.
Lecture-specific note
The page-16 heading says “Replication Process of Herpesviridae”, but the bullets and Figure 45 describe poxvirus replication.
This reviewer preserves the content as poxvirus replication and flags the source heading mismatch rather than silently ignoring it.

Poxvirus replication p. 16

  • The entire multiplication cycle occurs in the cytoplasm.
  • The virus supplies all required enzymes, including viral DNA-dependent RNA polymerase.
  • DNA polymerase and thymidine kinase are needed for DNA replication.
  • Virus attaches to the cell surface and fuses with the cell membrane. Viral cores are released into the cytoplasm.
  • Uncoating liberates viral DNA from the cores.
  • Late viral mRNA is translated into large amounts of structural proteins and enzymes.
  • Final maturation includes acquisition of a lipoprotein envelope as virus buds from the cell.
  • Replication is rapid and shuts off host macromolecular synthesis early, producing cell death.

Host-defense countermeasures encoded by poxvirus p. 17

The lecture states that poxvirus genes resemble mammalian genes and can inhibit host defenses by countering complement and cytokine networks. Listed examples are:

  • Tumor necrosis factor receptor.
  • Interferon-gamma receptor.
  • IL-1 receptor.
  • Complement-binding protein.

Smallpox or variola virus p. 17

Must know
Smallpox was the first viral disease eradicated worldwide.
The lecture states eradication in 1980.
Humans are the natural host and variola does not exist in a carrier state.

Transmission and infectious period p. 17

  • Variola is an acute contagious Orthopoxvirus disease.
  • It spread most efficiently through inhalation.
  • Direct contact with scabs or pustular lesion material and fomites were less efficient routes.
  • Respiratory droplets were infectious earlier than skin lesions.
  • Patients were highly infectious during the first week after the rash appeared, after fever had begun.
  • The lecture describes smallpox as a potentially devastating biological-warfare weapon because it is highly contagious and has a high case-fatality rate.

Clinical progression p. 17

  • Incubation is about 10 to 14 days.
  • Onset is acute, with 1 to 5 days of fever and malaise.
  • Exanthem then progresses through macules → papules → vesicles → pustules.
  • Smallpox lesions are in the same stage of development.
  • By contrast, chickenpox lesions occur in crops and can be at different stages at the same time.
Four types of smallpox
TypeLecture description
Variola minorCommon but less fatal.
Variola majorMore common and deadly.
Hemorrhagic smallpoxRare and deadly.
Organs leak blood into mucous membranes and skin.
Malignant smallpoxRare and deadly.
Lesions do not develop into pustules.
Lesions remain soft and flat throughout illness.

Immunity and laboratory diagnosis p. 17

  • Survival from smallpox confers complete protection in the lecture.
  • Vaccination with vaccinia induces immunity for at least 5 years and sometimes longer.
  • Specimen of choice is skin lesions.
  • Primary detection and identification method is PCR.
  • Confirmation can also include viral DNA or antigen detection from lesions, direct microscopy of skin-lesion material, virus recovery and, less importantly, antibody demonstration.
  • Rapid identification can use electron microscopy. Virus isolation can use cell culture or inoculation of vesicular fluid onto the chorioallantoic membrane of chick embryos.
  • Antibody methods listed include hemagglutination inhibition, neutralization, ELISA, radioimmunoassay and immunofluorescence.

Treatment and prevention p. 18

  • Treatment is primarily supportive care.
  • The lecture states that no treatment has been proven effective.
  • Cidofovir is listed as an experimental antiviral with activity against poxviruses in vitro and in vivo.
  • Vaccinia virus is the agent used for smallpox vaccination and is protective if given within 3 days of exposure.
  • Methisazone is described as historically evaluated, prophylactic but not curative.

Mpox, cowpox and molluscum contagiosum p. 18

Mpox p. 18

  • Formerly called monkeypox. It is caused by monkeypox virus, an Orthopoxvirus species.
  • The lecture describes it as a zoonosis detected in African settings and probably acquired through direct contact with wild animals killed for food or skins.
  • Clinical disease resembles smallpox but is less severe.
  • Pronounced cervical and submandibular lymphadenopathy is emphasized and is stated to be absent in smallpox and chickenpox.
  • Complications can be serious, including pulmonary distress and secondary bacterial infections.
  • Vaccinia can protect against mpox or reduce disease severity.
  • Person-to-person transmission is listed as skin-to-skin contact, mouth-to-skin contact during kissing and close breathing exposure.
  • Laboratory diagnosis: PCR.

Cowpox p. 18

  • Cowpox is another Orthopoxvirus. The natural reservoir is rodents, while cattle and humans are accidental hosts.
  • Disease is milder in cattle and mainly affects teats and udders. Domestic cats can also be infected.
  • Human infection occurs by direct contact during milking, with lesions usually on the hands.
  • Disease is more severe in unvaccinated persons than in people vaccinated with vaccinia.
  • The lecture recounts Jenner’s observation that milkmaids with prior cowpox were immune to smallpox.
  • Cowpox can be distinguished from vaccinia by a deep red hemorrhagic lesion.

Molluscum contagiosum p. 18

  • Humans are the natural host. The disease is a benign epidermal tumor found only in humans.
  • It is caused by the sole member of the Molluscipoxvirus genus.
  • The virus is a poor immunogen. About one third of patients never produce antibodies, so second attacks are common.
  • It is more common in children.
  • Lesions are single or multiple rounded, dome-shaped, pink waxy papules with central umbilication and a caseous plug.
  • Common sites are trunk, face, axilla, abdomen and thighs. Palms, soles and mucous membranes are rarely affected.
  • Scratching can cause autoinoculation. Lesions may persist up to 2 years but can regress spontaneously.
  • Spread occurs by direct or indirect contact with fomites such as barber implements, towels and swimming-pool exposures. Sexual transmission is also described, including in AIDS patients.

Molluscum diagnosis and treatment p. 19

  • Diagnosis is primarily clinical.
  • Caseous plug material can be used for laboratory diagnosis.
  • PCR detects viral DNA and electron microscopy can identify poxvirus particles.
  • Lecture-listed treatment: imiquimod cream.

Hepatitis B virus: structure, viability and replication p. 19

Core virology p. 19

  • HBV belongs to the Hepadnaviridae, a family of hepatitis-causing DNA viruses.
  • HBV is the only family member in the lecture that infects humans, causing serum hepatitis.
  • Chronic infection is especially likely after infection during infancy and is a major factor in chronic liver disease and hepatocellular carcinoma.
  • The virion is an enveloped icosahedral nucleocapsid.
  • The envelope contains HBsAg. The inner core contains HBcAg.
  • HBsAg is produced in excess by infected hepatocytes.
  • HBeAg is associated with the HBV nucleocapsid.
  • The genome is unusual: partly single-stranded, partly double-stranded, non-covalently closed circular DNA. One strand is longer and one is incomplete.
  • A DNA polymerase molecule is associated with the incomplete strand and can complete it when supplied with deoxynucleoside triphosphates.
HBV viability points from the lecture
ConditionLecture finding
37°C for 60 minutesHBV remains stable.
Dried at 25°CRemains viable for at least one week.
100°C for 1 minute or 60°C for 10 hoursHigher temperatures or prolonged heating reduce viability.
HBsAg at pH 2.4HBsAg remains stable for up to 6 hours, while infectivity is lost.
0.5% sodium hypochloriteDestroys HBV antigenicity within about 3 minutes.
Ultraviolet irradiationThe lecture states HBsAg is not destroyed by UV irradiation of plasma or other blood products.

Replication sequence p. 19

  • Virion attaches to the cell and uncoats.
  • The genome enters the nucleus.
  • Partially double-stranded relaxed circular DNA is converted to covalently closed circular double-stranded DNA or cccDNA.
  • cccDNA serves as the template for viral transcripts, including a free-genome RNA that is packaged with newly synthesized HBcAg.
  • Inside the core, viral polymerase creates a negative-strand DNA copy by reverse transcriptase activity.
  • The polymerase then synthesizes the positive DNA strand.
  • Cores bud through pre-Golgi membranes and acquire envelopes containing HBsAg, then exit the cell.
  • Some cores can return to the nucleus and initiate another replication cycle in the same cell.

Transmission, pathology and histopathology p. 19

Transmission and high-risk groups p. 19

  • Infectious HBV is present in body fluids including blood, semen, saliva and breast milk.
  • The lecture emphasizes infection at or shortly after birth from a chronically infected mother, or from infected siblings.
  • Early-life infection carries a substantial chance of becoming a chronic carrier and increases HCC risk.
  • Other routes include contaminated syringes, needles and scalpels, tattooing, ear piercing and sexual transmission.
  • High-risk groups listed are parenteral drug users, institutionalized persons, healthcare personnel, multiply transfused patients, organ-transplant patients, hemodialysis patients, highly promiscuous persons and newborns of mothers with hepatitis B.

Liver injury mechanism p. 20

  • The primary infected cell is the fully differentiated hepatocyte.
  • The lecture identifies the primary cause of hepatocyte destruction as the cell-mediated immune response, rather than direct viral cytolysis.
  • Cytotoxic T cells react to fragments of nucleocapsid proteins, including HBcAg and HBeAg, expressed at the surface of infected hepatocytes.

Histopathology p. 20

  • Spotty parenchymal degeneration and hepatocyte necrosis.
  • Diffuse lobular inflammatory reaction with disruption of liver-cell cords.
  • Reticuloendothelial or Kupffer-cell hyperplasia.
  • Periportal mononuclear-cell infiltration and cell degeneration.
  • Localized necrosis may occur.
  • Preservation of the reticulum framework allows hepatocyte regeneration. The lecture states damaged hepatic tissue is usually restored in 8 to 12 weeks.
  • Chronic active hepatitis may progress from inflammation and necrosis to collapse of the normal reticulum framework with bridging between portal triads or terminal hepatic veins.
  • Ground-glass hepatocytes in chronic HBV represent accumulation of viral antigen in the endoplasmic reticulum.

Clinical course and antigen-antibody kinetics p. 20

Clinical presentation p. 20

  • Incubation is 45 to 120 days.
  • The preicteric phase lasts several days to about a week and includes mild fever, malaise, anorexia and nausea.
  • The acute icteric phase lasts about 1 to 2 months, with dark urine from bilirubinuria, jaundice and an enlarged tender liver.
  • Most adult patients then enter a several-month convalescent period and recover completely.
Sequence of HBV markers in the lecture
PhaseMarker behavior and interpretation
IncubationHBsAg and HBeAg are the first indicators to appear in blood.
Their presence indicates active infection but does not by itself distinguish acute from chronic infection.
HBeAg indicates active viral replication and infectivity.
Acute diseaseViral DNA, DNA polymerase and complete virions become detectable and rise.
Anti-HBc rises along with serum liver enzymes.
ConvalescenceAnti-HBe and anti-HBs appear after their respective antigens disappear.
Window periodHBsAg has fallen but anti-HBs has not yet appeared.
The lecture’s simplified pattern lists anti-HBc and anti-HBe as positive.
Resolved infectionAnti-HBc and anti-HBs remain for life in the lecture and provide immunity to reinfection.

Chronic infection and hepatocellular carcinoma p. 20

Progression patterns p. 20

  • Chronic infection is defined by persistence of hepatitis B antigen beyond 6 months with absence of anti-HBs.
  • Fulminant hepatitis can occur in acute symptomatic disease. The lecture describes extensive necrosis during the first 8 weeks with high fever, abdominal pain, renal dysfunction, coma and seizures. It can be fatal.
  • Possible contributors listed for fulminant disease are a more virulent HBV strain, hepatitis D or other hepatitis-virus coinfection, and uncontrolled host immune response.
  • Some primary infections are asymptomatic but still persist and later produce chronic liver disease.
  • Asymptomatic HBsAg carriers are the most common persistently infected group in the lecture and usually have anti-HBe.
  • Minimal chronic hepatitis is usually asymptomatic, but has greater reactivation risk and a small risk of progression to cirrhosis.
  • Severe chronic hepatitis has more frequent exacerbations and progressive liver damage that can end in cirrhosis or HCC. Active replication is associated with HBeAg.
  • The risk of cirrhosis is greatest with frequent late recurrences and failure to clear HBeAg.
  • HCC develops many years after primary infection. Clinical features listed are weight loss, right-upper-quadrant pain, fever and intestinal bleeding.

HBV antigens, antibodies and serology p. 21

HBV antigen and antibody meaning
MarkerMeaning in the lecture
HBsAgFirst serum marker detected after initial infection.
Presence always implies active infection.
Persistence beyond 6 months indicates chronic infection.
Anti-HBsAppears with HBsAg seroconversion and indicates clearance or vaccination when HBsAg is negative.
Remains for life in the lecture and indicates immunity.
The lecture gives >10 to 12 mIU/mL as protective.
HBcAgCore antigen in the nucleocapsid.
Not the protein measured in routine clinical practice.
Anti-HBc IgMRecent infection within the last 6 months.
Anti-HBc IgGResolved or chronic infection.
HBeAgPresent in active acute and chronic infection.
Serum presence indicates active viral replication and high transmissibility.
Anti-HBeRemains in serum for life in the lecture and indicates natural immunity from previous infection only.

High viral load is linked to higher risk of cirrhosis and HCC and is expected in active chronic disease.
Lecture-specific inconsistency
The page-21 text states that HBeAg indicates active viral replication and high transmissibility.
The same subsection also contains the line “(+) HBsAg (+) HBeAg = transition from active to inactive disease carrier state.”
These statements do not align cleanly. This reviewer preserves both source statements and flags the inconsistency rather than resolving it with outside information.
Simplified HBV serology patterns stated in the lecture
InterpretationHBsAgAnti-HBsAnti-HBcHBeAgAnti-HBe
No past or present infection−−−−−
Incubation stage+−−−−
Acute hepatitis B+−IgM ++−
Chronic replicating HBV+−++−

If you see this
Anti-HBs only → vaccination response.
HBsAg + IgM anti-HBc + HBeAg → acute hepatitis B in the lecture’s review examples.
HBsAg + anti-HBc IgG + anti-HBe → chronic non-replicating pattern.

HBV diagnosis, treatment and prevention p. 21

Diagnostic anchors p. 21

  • Most useful methods named are ELISA for antigens and antibodies and PCR for viral DNA.
  • HBV infection can also elevate ALT, AST and bilirubin.
HBV treatment hierarchy in the lecture
LineDrugLecture mechanism or effect
First linePegylated interferon alpha-2aLong-acting.
Decreases hepatitis B DNA.
First lineEntecavirInhibits HBV polymerase and can make HBV DNA undetectable.
First lineTenofovirNucleotide analog inhibitor of HBV reverse transcriptase and polymerase.
Useful in treatment-naive patients and in resistance to lamivudine, telbivudine or entecavir.
Second lineTelbivudineHBV polymerase inhibitor listed as second-line therapy.
Third lineLamivudine and adefovirHBV polymerase inhibitors listed as third-line therapies.

When treatment is used p. 21

  • The lecture states that treatment is usually not needed in more than 95% of adults because the immune system controls and eliminates infection within 6 months.
  • Treatment is used in chronic hepatitis B to prevent progression and complications such as cirrhosis and HCC.

Prevention and control p. 22

  • Use universal precautions for body fluids potentially contaminated with HBV.
  • Avoid needle-stick injury and contact with mucous membranes or non-intact skin. Use PPE and discard disposable needles appropriately.
  • Decontaminate work areas with bleach solution. The lecture prohibits mouth pipetting, smoking, eating and drinking in work areas.
  • Public-health measures include universal infant vaccination, routine HBsAg screening in pregnancy, post-exposure immunoprophylaxis for infants born to HBsAg-positive mothers, and vaccination of children, adolescents and adults including immunosuppressed persons.
  • Recombinant DNA-derived hepatitis B vaccine is the most effective pre-exposure preventive measure in the lecture.
  • Hepatitis B immunoglobulin or HBIg is used after exposure such as needle-stick injury or mucosal contamination.
  • The lecture states that HBIg and hepatitis B vaccine should be given simultaneously at different sites after qualifying exposure, to provide immediate passive protection followed by active immunity.
  • This vaccine-plus-HBIg approach is documented as effective for infants born to HBV-positive mothers.

Classic rash and lesion differentiators
ConditionPattern emphasized in lectureExtra clue
Fifth diseaseSlapped-cheek erythema followed by fine lacy maculopapular rash on trunk and limbs.B19.
Patient is no longer infectious once antibody-associated rash stage occurs in the immunocompetent host.
VaricellaFresh lesions appear in crops. Macules, papules, vesicles and crusts coexist.Primary VZV.
Herpes zosterPainful vesicles in a unilateral dermatomal pattern.Reactivated VZV.
SmallpoxLesions in the same stage of development.Eradicated in 1980.
MpoxSmallpox-like but less severe.Cervical and submandibular lymphadenopathy, unlike smallpox or chickenpox.
Molluscum contagiosumDome-shaped pink waxy umbilicated papules with caseous plug.May persist up to 2 years then regress.
Viral replication location and special dependency
Virus or familyMain location in lectureSpecial replication clue
ParvovirusNucleusDepends on host cell entering S phase.
AdenovirusNucleusEarly phase induces S phase. Late genes produce structural proteins.
HerpesviridaeNucleus for DNA replication and capsid packagingDNA circles after uncoating. Envelope acquired by budding through nuclear membrane.
PoxviridaeCytoplasmVirion supplies its own enzymes including DNA-dependent RNA polymerase.
HBVNuclear cccDNA plus reverse transcription in corePartially dsDNA becomes cccDNA, then RNA intermediate is reverse-transcribed.

Cancer-associated DNA viruses in this lecture
VirusCancer associations emphasized
HPVCervical, anal, penile, vaginal, vulvar and oropharyngeal cancers.
High-risk E6 and E7 are primary oncoproteins.

Naked DNA viruses
Parvovirus B19: smallest DNA virus, ss linear DNA, erythroid progenitors, P-antigen, S-phase dependence.
Adenovirus: ds linear DNA, epithelial disease, vaRNA blocks interferon effects, E3 gp19 kDa blocks MHC I surface movement.
HPV: ds circular DNA, surface epithelium only, high-risk E6/E7 target p53 and pRb.
JCV: PML through cytocidal oligodendrocyte infection.
Parvovirus must-knows
Fifth disease = most common B19 manifestation.
Slapped cheek → lacy trunk and limb rash.
Immunodeficient: pure red cell aplasia.
Pregnancy: non-immune fetal hydrops or fetal loss from anemia.
Sickle cell or thalassemia: aplastic crisis.
No vaccine or antiviral drug in the lecture.
Adenovirus must-knows
Types 4 and 7: acute respiratory disease in military recruits.
Types 3 and 7: pharyngoconjunctival or swimming-pool conjunctivitis.
Types 8, 19 and 37: epidemic keratoconjunctivitis.
Types 40 and 41: infantile gastroenteritis.
One serotype can cause different syndromes and several serotypes can cause the same syndrome.
HPV must-knows
HPV 6 and 11: 90% of anogenital warts and laryngeal papillomas.
HPV 16 and 18: over 70% of cervical cancers in the lecture.
Persistent high-risk HPV is necessary for malignant progression.
E6 and E7 are the primary oncoproteins.
Pap smear remains a cervical-screening tool regardless of vaccination status.
HSV must-knows
Oropharyngeal HSV → trigeminal ganglion.
Genital HSV → sacral ganglion.
HSV-1: lecture’s most common cause of sporadic fatal encephalitis in the US.
CSF PCR: test of choice and gold standard for herpes meningitis and encephalitis.
Asymptomatic shedding can transmit genital herpes.
VZV must-knows
Varicella = primary VZV.
Zoster = reactivation.
Varicella lesions appear in crops with several stages at once.
Zoster is painful and dermatomal.
NAAT = gold standard.
Start antiviral therapy within 24 to 48 hours of symptoms.
EBV must-knows
IM triad: fever, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy.
Major target: B lymphocyte using the C3d receptor.
Large atypical T cells = Downey cells.
EBV associations: Burkitt lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphoma, gastric carcinoma.
EBER ISH = tissue gold standard.
CMV must-knows
Owl’s-eye inclusions.
Mono-like illness is heterophile-antibody negative.
Most common intrauterine viral infection in the lecture.
Congenital CMV: jaundice, petechiae, hepatosplenomegaly, nervous-system injury.
CMV mnemonic: Chorioretinitis, Microcephalia/Mental/Motor retardation, periVentricular calcifications.
NAAT = standard test.
HHV-6, 7 and 8
HHV-6: sudden high fever, then macular rash when fever resolves. HHV-6B is major roseola cause. CD46 is the receptor.
HHV-7: can cause roseola but more often asymptomatic. Persistent in salivary glands.
HHV-8: Kaposi sarcoma herpesvirus. Oral secretions are the most common route listed.
Pox must-knows
Poxviruses replicate entirely in the cytoplasm.
Smallpox: eradicated in 1980, no carrier state, same-stage lesions.
Mpox: cervical and submandibular lymphadenopathy distinguishes it from smallpox and chickenpox in the lecture.
Molluscum: pink waxy dome-shaped umbilicated papules with caseous plug.
HBV must-knows
HBsAg: active infection. Persistence beyond 6 months = chronic infection.
HBeAg: active replication and high transmissibility in the main lecture statement.
Anti-HBc IgM: recent infection within 6 months.
Anti-HBs only: vaccination response.
HBsAg + IgM anti-HBc + HBeAg: acute hepatitis B.
HBV replication: cccDNA in nucleus plus reverse transcription in the core.
